::: callout-note
This is my own Component 2, written as a model for yours. It picks up where [my Component 1](project1_example_byrd.html) left off. My data is an HTML page, so my cleaning has more steps than most of yours will. Focus on the overall shape: read, clean into a Python structure, build a `DataFrame`, check it, save, reload.
:::

## 1. The Raw Data

My raw data is the online version of Julius Pokorny's *Indogermanisches etymologisches Wörterbuch* (1959), scanned by George Starostin, with English meanings added by him and corrections by Alexander Lubotsky and the site's maintainer:

-   <https://aeb.win.tue.nl/natlang/ie/pokorny.html>

The whole dictionary is one very large web page. I opened its source (`view-source:` in the browser), copied all of it, and pasted it into a file called `pokorny_site.txt` in my `course_project` folder. I didn't change anything by hand after that.

One change since Component 1: I'd planned to copy the *visible* text of the page, but I switched to the HTML source. The source has tags like `<h1>` and `<b>English</b>` that mark exactly where each entry and each field begins, and that makes the splitting much more reliable than guessing from the visible text.

::: callout-warning
## Copyright

The printed IEW is still under copyright, so `pokorny_site.txt` is listed in my `.gitignore` and isn't in my public repo. My `.csv` also contains a lot of the dictionary's text (see Section 3), so it's kept out of the repo too.
:::

Let's read it in:

```{python}
import re
from collections import Counter
import pandas as pd

with open("pokorny_site.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    raw = f.read()

print(len(raw))
print(raw[:300])
```

That's almost 5 million characters, starting with some HTML boilerplate. Here's what one entry looks like in the source (entry 2, shortened):

``` html
<h1>    2. <b><i><a name="ab-">ab-</a></i></b></h1>
<p><b>English</b>   : ‘water, river’
<p><b>German</b>    : ‘Wasser, Fluß’
<p><b>Material</b>  : Lat. <i>amnis</i> f., später m. ...; air. <i>ab</i> ...
<p><b>Ref</b>       : WP. I 46 f., WH. I 40, ...
<p><b>Page</b>     : 1
<p><b>PIET</b>      :    0
```

So every entry starts with `<h1>`, and every field starts with `<p><b>Label</b> :`. Those two patterns are what I'll split on.

## 2. Cleaning Steps

### Step 1: Superscripts and subscripts

Before splitting, I have to deal with one problem. Pokorny uses superscripts and subscripts *inside* root forms, e.g. `ab<sub>e</sub>l-` (a reduced vowel) and `ba<sup>x</sup>b-`. These tags sometimes show up inside other tags, and that breaks the tag-removal regex I use later. But they're also part of Pokorny's notation, so I don't want to just delete them.

Luckily, Unicode has subscript and superscript versions of most of the characters Pokorny uses: `ₑ`, `ₒ`, `ₔ`, `ˣ`, `²`... So I make two lookup dictionaries, from each ordinary character to its subscript or superscript version:

```{python}
sub_chars = {"a": "ₐ", "e": "ₑ", "o": "ₒ", "u": "ᵤ", "ə": "ₔ", "(": "₍", ")": "₎"}

sup_chars = {"0": "⁰", "1": "¹", "2": "²", "3": "³", "4": "⁴",
             "5": "⁵", "6": "⁶", "7": "⁷", "8": "⁸", "9": "⁹",
             "a": "ᵃ", "b": "ᵇ", "e": "ᵉ", "f": "ᶠ", "h": "ʰ", "i": "ⁱ", "m": "ᵐ",
             "n": "ⁿ", "o": "ᵒ", "r": "ʳ", "s": "ˢ", "u": "ᵘ", "v": "ᵛ", "x": "ˣ",
             "z": "ᶻ", "ə": "ᵊ", "(": "⁽", ")": "⁾"}
```

Then, for every different thing that appears between `<sub>` and `</sub>`, I build its subscript version one character at a time and swap it in, tags and all. `.get(ch, ch)` means "look up `ch`, and if it isn't in the dictionary, just keep `ch`." The same goes for superscripts.

```{python}
for inside in set(re.findall(r"<sub>(.*?)</sub>", raw)):
    new = ""
    for ch in inside:
        new = new + sub_chars.get(ch, ch)
    raw = raw.replace("<sub>" + inside + "</sub>", new)

for inside in set(re.findall(r"<sup>(.*?)</sup>", raw)):
    new = ""
    for ch in inside:
        new = new + sup_chars.get(ch, ch)
    raw = raw.replace("<sup>" + inside + "</sup>", new)

print("<sub>" in raw, "<sup>" in raw)
```

Now `ab<sub>e</sub>l-` is `abₑl-`, and `ba<sup>x</sup>b-` is `baˣb-`. Most of the superscripts in the Material are footnote and edition numbers (`WP.²`), and they come through as `²`, `³`, and so on.

*What this costs me:* two characters have no superscript version in Unicode, the asterisk (Pokorny's footnote mark) and one stray semicolon, so they stay ordinary characters. And for searching, `abₑl-` is now a different string from `abel-`. If I search the roots for `el` in Component 3, I'll miss this one unless I plan for it.

### Step 2: Split into entries

Splitting on `<h1>` gives one chunk per entry. The first piece (`[0]`) is everything *before* the first entry, which is the page header, so I throw it away with `[1:]`.

```{python}
chunks = re.split(r"<h1>", raw)[1:]
print(len(chunks))
```

2,222 entries, which is exactly what the dictionary's own numbering goes up to.

### Step 3: Build a nested dictionary

Now I go through each chunk and pull it apart into a dictionary of dictionaries. The **key** is the entry number, and the **value** is a dictionary of that entry's fields:

``` python
iew[2] = {"forms": "ab-", "English": "‘water, river’", "German": "‘Wasser, Fluß’", ...}
```

I use the entry number as the key, not the root, because Pokorny has many homonyms (`ad-1`, `ad-2`), and because numbers sort correctly.

For each chunk, the header is everything before `</h1>`, and the body is everything after. To clean up each piece, I remove the HTML tags with `re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", ...)` (a `<`, then anything that isn't `>`, then `>`), and squash runs of spaces and line breaks down to a single space with `re.sub(r"\s+", " ", ...)`.

To split the body into fields, I use `re.split()` with a **capturing group** `(...)` around the label. That keeps the labels in the result, so `parts` alternates: the text before the first label, then label, value, label, value... That means the labels are at positions 1, 3, 5..., and each value comes right after its label. `range(1, len(parts), 2)` counts 1, 3, 5... for me.

```{python}
iew = {}

for chunk in chunks:
    head, body = chunk.split("</h1>", 1)
    head = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", head).strip()     # e.g. "2. ab-"
    number, forms = head.split(". ", 1)

    entry = {"forms": forms}
    parts = re.split(r"<p><b>([^<]+)</b>\s*:", body)
    for i in range(1, len(parts), 2):
        label = parts[i].strip()
        value = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", parts[i + 1])    # remove tags
        value = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", value).strip()     # tidy whitespace
        entry[label] = value

    iew[int(number)] = entry

print(len(iew))
iew[2]
```

### Step 4: Check the fields

Which labels did I find, and how often?

```{python}
label_counts = Counter()
for entry in iew.values():
    label_counts.update(entry.keys())

label_counts.most_common()
```

Three things jump out:

-   `Page` and `Pages` are the same field under two different labels (`Pages` is used when an entry runs over more than one page). I'll merge them.
-   Every entry has `PIET`, but only 2,077 have `English`. What are the other 145?

```{python}
no_english = [num for num, entry in iew.items() if "English" not in entry]
print(len(no_english))
iew[no_english[0]]
```

They're **cross-references**: entries like *aĝro-s* whose only content is "s. aĝ-" ("see *aĝ-*"). They aren't real roots, so I'm dropping them.

```{python}
roots = {}
for num, entry in iew.items():
    if "English" in entry:
        roots[num] = entry

print(len(roots))
```

## 3. The Clean Table

Now I build one row per root. Just like in class, I make a **list of dicts**, one dict per row, and hand it to `pd.DataFrame()`. The entry number goes in its own `entry` column, so it's saved with the data. Two last fixes happen along the way:

-   Pokorny puts meanings in curly quotes (‘water, river’). I remove the quote marks around them, using a capturing group again: `‘([^’]*)’` matches a whole quoted stretch, and `r"\1"` puts back just what was inside. Apostrophes in the middle of a meaning are left alone.
-   `Page` and `Pages` become one `page` column. When an entry runs over several pages (`1-2`), I keep the first page number, so the column can be a number. `re.split(r"\D", ...)` splits on anything that isn't a digit, and `[0]` takes the first piece.

```{python}
rows = []

for num, entry in roots.items():
    english = re.sub(r"‘([^’]*)’", r"\1", entry["English"])
    german = re.sub(r"‘([^’]*)’", r"\1", entry.get("German", ""))
    pages = entry.get("Page", entry.get("Pages", ""))
    page = int(re.split(r"\D", pages)[0])

    rows.append({
        "entry": num,
        "forms": entry["forms"],
        "english": english.strip(),
        "german": german.strip(),
        "material": entry.get("Material", ""),
        "page": page,
    })

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
df.head()
```

Checking it over:

```{python}
print(len(df))
df.tail()
```

2,077 rows, one per root. The last row is entry 2222, *u̯rughi̯o-* 'rye', the last entry on the page, so nothing got cut off at the end.

One row represents one **root entry** in Pokorny. The columns:

| Column | What it is |
|-------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `entry` | Pokorny's entry number |
| `forms` | the root, with any variants, as Pokorny lists them (e.g. `ā̆bel-, ā̆bōl-, abel-`) |
| `english` | Starostin's English meaning |
| `german` | Pokorny's German meaning |
| `material` | the daughter-language words, as one long string of German text |
| `page` | first page of the entry in the printed IEW |

I left out the `Ref`, `Comments`, `See also`, `Derivative`, `Grammar` and `PIET` fields. They're scholarly references and notes that I don't need for my questions, and they're still in my `iew` dictionary if I change my mind.

I kept `material`, even though it's long and messy, because my question about which branches attest each root depends on it. That also means my `.csv` contains a big chunk of the dictionary's actual text, so the `.csv` is in my `.gitignore` too, just like the raw file.

### Save and Reload

```{python}
df.to_csv("project2_byrd_andrew.csv", index=False, encoding="utf-8-sig")

check = pd.read_csv("project2_byrd_andrew.csv")
print(len(df), len(check))
check.head()
```

Same number of rows (2,077), same six columns, and the special characters survive. One difference: the five roots with no `material` come back with `NaN` (pandas' "nothing here") instead of an empty string. I'll need to deal with that when I start searching `material` in Component 3.

## 4. Still Messy

-   **Several forms per entry.** The `forms` column often holds more than one form, and sometimes notes like `oder` ('or') and question marks. To ask how roots begin, I'll need to pick one form per entry.
-   **Notation.** Forms are full of diacritics and special symbols: `ĝ`, `k̂`, `kʷ`, `u̯`, `ə`, the s-mobile `(s)`, homonym numbers like `ad-1`. I'll have to decide which of these count as separate sounds.
-   **The material is unstructured.** Languages are marked only by abbreviations inside German prose (`ai.`, `lat.`, `ags.`...). Some look misleading: `skr.` in Pokorny is *serbokroatisch*, Serbo-Croatian, not Sanskrit (that's `ai.`, *altindisch*). I'll need a lookup table from abbreviation to branch.
-   **Five roots have no material.** Some of them, like *u̯er-* 'to turn, bend', have their words listed under their root extensions, which have their own entries.
-   **Subscript and superscript letters.** Forms like `abₑl-` and `baˣb-` keep Pokorny's notation, but they won't match a search for plain `abel-` or `bab-`. I'll have to decide how to treat them before searching the roots.
-   **The English meanings vary in style** (`to swell`, `a k. of big fish`, `indefinite/interrogative pronominal base`), which will matter when I get to WordNet.
